set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What does the canal look like in ACUTE otitis externa?
opts: Swollen, narrow, moist, pale and tender, and it may be erythematous
Correct. The swelling and tenderness dominate, and the narrowing is often what makes the examination difficult.
Thickened, red and itchy
That is the CHRONIC picture. The acute canal is swollen and painful rather than thickened and itchy.
Dry, scaly and pale, with no tenderness
Tenderness is a defining feature of the acute form.
Normal, with the abnormality confined to the tympanic membrane
Otitis externa is a disease of the canal, which is precisely how it is distinguished from middle ear disease.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: The Weber test is done and the patient hears the tone only in the LEFT ear. Which ear has sensorineural hearing loss?
opts: Neither — this is a normal result
A normal result is midline or equal in both ears.
Both
Weber evaluates unilateral loss; a bilateral symmetrical loss would not lateralise.
The right
Correct. Sensorineural loss lateralises AWAY from the damaged side, so hearing the tone on the left places the lesion on the right.
The left
That would be true for a conductive loss, which lateralises TOWARD the affected side.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: FINE hair and COARSE hair on examination point to which conditions?
opts: Fine hair to hyperthyroidism; coarse hair to hypothyroidism
Correct — a small finding, but it is examined for at the same moment as the scalp and the skull.
Fine hair to hypothyroidism; coarse hair to hyperthyroidism
Reversed. The pale bluish mucosa is the allergic picture; viral rhinitis makes it red and swollen.
Both to hypothyroidism
The two textures point in opposite directions.
Both to nutritional deficiency
The association given is with thyroid status.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Hard nodules on the auricle made of uric acid crystals. What are they, and what do they indicate?
opts: Keloids, indicating previous trauma
Keloids are scar tissue and contain no crystal.
Cutaneous cysts, indicating follicular obstruction
Cysts are epidermoid or pilar, and are not crystalline.
Exostoses, indicating repeated cold water exposure
Exostoses are bony growths in the canal, not nodules on the auricle.
Tophi, indicating chronic tophaceous gout
Correct. They are deposits rather than growths, and finding them on the ear points to long-standing disease.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Why does a septal haematoma require URGENT drainage?
opts: To prevent secondary sinusitis
Infection can follow, but cartilage necrosis is the stated reason.
To prevent necrosis of the septal cartilage
Correct. The cartilage has no blood supply of its own — it depends on the lining that the haematoma has stripped away, so the clock starts immediately.
To prevent the blood tracking into the orbit
Blood tracking into the orbit is not the reason given; the cartilage has no blood supply of its own and dies without its lining.
To prevent airway obstruction
Obstruction may occur but is not why the drainage is urgent.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Which part of the hand is used to palpate the lymph nodes of the neck?
opts: The pads of the index and middle fingers
Correct. The pads are the most sensitive surface, and two fingers cover a node without rolling past it.
The fingertips of all four fingers
The technique specifies the pads of two fingers.
The thumb and index finger in a pincer grip
Shining the light into the nostril tests nothing; the maxillary sinus is lit from below the medial canthus.
The ulnar border of the hand
That is the otoscopy anchoring point, not a palpation surface.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What is needed to inspect the POSTERIOR pharynx properly?
opts: An otoscope with the largest speculum
The otoscope is for the ear canal.
A nasal speculum
Used for the nose.
Transillumination in a dark room
That is the sinus technique.
A tongue blade
Correct. The tongue obscures the posterior wall and has to be depressed out of the way.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Why should recent dental work be asked about when a patient presents with facial pain?
opts: Dental work is a recognised cause of epistaxis
The epistaxis causes given are trauma, inflammation, dry mucosa, foreign body and tumour.
Dental infection is the commonest cause of frontal sinusitis
The named relationship is with the MAXILLARY sinuses.
Dental work may affect the maxillary sinuses
Correct. The maxillary sinus floor sits directly above the upper tooth roots, so a dental procedure can present as sinus pain.
Dental anaesthetic commonly causes anosmia
Anosmia is asked about separately in the nose history; it is not tied to dental anaesthetic.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What causes a PERFORATED nasal septum?
opts: A foreign body lodged for several days
A retained foreign body causes unilateral obstruction and foul discharge; the three causes of perforation given are trauma, surgery and drug use.
Repeated epistaxis from Kiesselbach's plexus
Bleeding from the anterior septum does not itself perforate it.
Trauma, surgery or drug use
Correct. All three destroy the septal blood supply or the cartilage itself, and drug use is the one patients do not volunteer.
Allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis
Allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis inflame the mucosa without destroying the cartilage underneath it.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What does bleeding of the gums suggest?
opts: Vitamin B12 deficiency
B12 deficiency is linked to a smooth, beefy red TONGUE.
Necrotising ulcerative gingivitis only
That is a specific severe entity; ordinary bleeding gums point to gingivitis generally.
Oral carcinoma
Oral cancer presents as an indurated red or white lesion, usually lateral or under the tongue.
Gingivitis
Correct. Bleeding gums point to gingivitis — inflammation of the gum margin itself.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Endemic goitre is associated with what?
opts: Previous radiation exposure
Radiation exposure raises thyroid cancer risk; endemic goitre is attributed to dietary iodine deficiency.
Iodine deficiency
Correct. Endemic means it clusters geographically, and the reason is dietary iodine.
Autoimmune destruction of the gland
That is Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Thyroid-stimulating antibodies
Those drive Graves disease.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: An abnormally ENLARGED head raises which two conditions?
opts: Microcephaly and hydrocephalus
Microcephaly is an abnormally SMALL head.
Hypothyroidism and acromegaly
Hypothyroidism and acromegaly change facial appearance and hair; the two causes of an enlarged skull given are hydrocephalus and Paget disease.
Paget disease and microcephaly
Microcephaly belongs with small head size.
Hydrocephalus and Paget disease
Correct. One expands the skull from within, the other thickens the bone itself.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A headache of SUDDEN, SEVERE onset should raise which diagnosis?
opts: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Correct. Sudden and severe is the pattern that cannot be attributed to a benign cause without investigation.
Tension headache
Tension headache is episodic and not sudden and severe.
Migraine
Migraine is episodic and typically builds rather than peaking instantly.
Cluster headache
Cluster headache is severe and unilateral, but the sudden-and-severe pattern is given for subarachnoid haemorrhage.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A sore AND SMOOTH tongue suggests what?
opts: Oral candidiasis
Candidal infection gives plaques rather than a smooth surface.
Nutritional deficiency
Correct. The smoothness is loss of papillae, and that combination of sore and smooth is the pointer.
Aphthous ulceration
Aphthous ulcers are discrete painful lesions, not diffuse smoothing.
Geographic tongue
Geographic tongue is a benign pattern of map-like patches, and it is not smooth.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What is a NORMAL Weber result?
opts: Heard only through bone conduction
Weber is a bone conduction test throughout; the finding is where the sound goes, not how it travels.
Not heard at all
A normal patient hears it.
Midline, or heard equally in both ears
Correct. There is no lateralisation to report when both sides transmit equally.
Lateralised to the right
Any lateralisation is abnormal in a patient with unilateral loss.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A smooth, beefy red tongue points to which deficiency?
opts: Vitamin B12
Correct. The appearance is atrophic glossitis, and it earns a look for the rest of the deficiency picture.
Vitamin C
Vitamin C deficiency affects the gums rather than the tongue surface; the smooth beefy red tongue is attributed to B12.
Iron alone
Iron deficiency has its own oral signs, but the smooth beefy red tongue is attributed to vitamin B12.
Vitamin D
No such oral sign is given.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A patient says they are “dizzy”. Which four categories must the history separate?
opts: Orthostatic, cardiac, neurological and metabolic
A reasonable clinical list, but it splits by mechanism rather than by what the patient is actually describing.
Vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium and psychiatric causes
Correct. The word means nothing until the patient explains it, and these are the four things it turns out to mean.
Vertigo, migraine, seizure and syncope
Migraine and seizure are not the four categories given for the word “dizziness”.
Peripheral vertigo, central vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss
This splits vertigo into its own subtypes but omits the non-vestibular causes, which is the whole reason for asking.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Which two situations can the tuning fork tests NOT distinguish?
opts: Presbycusis from noise-induced loss
Neither test attempts to identify a cause; that is not the stated limitation.
Normal hearing from bilateral sensorineural loss, and normal hearing from mixed conductive and sensorineural loss
Correct. Both tests work by comparing sides or routes, so a loss that is symmetrical or that affects both routes leaves the comparison looking normal.
Conductive from sensorineural loss
That is precisely what they DO distinguish — it is the stated purpose of the tests.
Right-sided from left-sided loss
The Weber test exists to answer exactly that.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A patient speaks unusually SOFTLY despite a hearing complaint. Which loss does that point to?
opts: Conductive — the inner ear and cochlear nerve are intact, so the patient hears their own voice normally
Correct, and bone conduction of their own voice is if anything enhanced, so they have no reason to speak up.
Sensorineural — the patient compensates by speaking quietly
The opposite: sensorineural loss makes the voice LOUD.
Mixed loss only
Soft voice is given as a feature of the conductive pattern.
Presbycusis specifically
Presbycusis is sensorineural, and would make the voice loud.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A firm raised lesion at an old ear piercing site. Which finding is it, and who is most prone to it?
opts: A cutaneous cyst — more common in darker-skinned individuals
Cutaneous cysts are usually epidermoid or pilar and carry no such association.
Basal cell carcinoma — more common in darker-skinned individuals
Basal cell carcinoma is a malignancy, and the association runs the other way.
A keloid — scar tissue, more common in darker-skinned individuals
Correct. Keloids are commonest on the shoulders and upper chest but arise at piercing sites, which puts them on the ear.
Tophi — and there is no skin-type association
Tophi are uric acid deposits of chronic tophaceous gout, not related to piercing.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Why does the ABSENCE of cough count toward the Centor score rather than its presence?
opts: Cough is a criterion only in children
The criterion applies as stated, and it is absence that scores.
A cough points toward a viral cause, so its absence raises the probability of streptococcal infection
Correct. The rule is built to separate bacterial from viral pharyngitis, and cough is the most useful viral marker in the set.
Coughing masks tonsillar exudates on examination
Not the reasoning; the criterion is diagnostic, not technical.
A cough indicates the infection has spread to the lower airway
The criterion is about separating bacterial from viral pharyngitis, not about tracking spread to the lower airway.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A diffusely enlarged, FIRM thyroid points to what?
opts: Graves disease
Graves gives a SOFT diffuse enlargement.
A multinodular goitre
That is nodular rather than diffuse.
Thyroid carcinoma
A single hard nodule would raise that, not diffuse firm enlargement.
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Correct. Firmness is the feature that separates it from Graves, where the gland is soft.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Under what symptom duration is acute BACTERIAL sinusitis unlikely?
opts: Less than twelve weeks
Twelve weeks defines chronic disease.
Less than seven days
Correct. Most cases under a week are viral, which is the single most useful piece of timing in the nose section.
Less than three days
The stated threshold is seven days.
Less than four weeks
Four weeks is the boundary between acute and subacute disease, not the bacterial threshold.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What usually causes a tympanic membrane perforation, and what may accompany it?
opts: Otitis media, and drainage may come through the perforation
Correct. The perforation is usually the consequence of middle ear disease rather than a primary event.
Otitis externa, with itching through the perforation
Otitis externa is confined to the canal and does not perforate the membrane.
Barotrauma, with vertigo through the perforation
Pressure change is listed with serous effusion, not as the usual cause of perforation.
Cerumen impaction, with pain through the perforation
Wax blocks the canal; it does not perforate the membrane.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: How is nasal patency tested?
opts: Ask the patient to blow the nose and listen for asymmetry
Blowing the nose tells you nothing about which side is obstructed. Each nostril is occluded in turn and the patient breathes in.
Hold a mirror under the nose and compare the two areas of condensation
A mirror would show condensation from both nostrils together; the test isolates one side at a time.
Transilluminate each nostril in a dark room
Transillumination assesses the SINUSES, not patency.
Occlude one nostril and ask the patient to breathe in
Correct. Each side is tested separately, because unilateral obstruction is what carries the worrying differential.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: What are exostoses, and which type of hearing loss do they cause?
opts: Benign bony growths in the ear canal, causing conductive loss
Correct. They narrow the canal mechanically, which is why the loss is conductive.
Benign bony growths on the ossicles, causing sensorineural loss
They are canal growths, and any canal problem produces conductive loss.
Malignant bone tumours of the temporal bone
Exostoses are described as benign bony growths. A malignant temporal bone tumour is a different problem entirely.
Cholesterol deposits in the middle ear
Cholesterol collections in the middle ear are cholesteatomas. Exostoses are bone, and they sit in the canal.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: A normal Rinne on the right, and the Weber lateralises to the right. Where is the lesion and what type is it?
opts: Sensorineural loss in the right ear
Sensorineural loss lateralises AWAY from the affected side, so a right-sided lesion would send the Weber left.
Conductive loss in the left ear
Left conductive loss would also lateralise Weber to the left, not the right.
Sensorineural loss in the LEFT ear
Correct. A normal Rinne rules out conductive loss on the side tested, and Weber lateralising right places the sensorineural damage on the left. This was the worked case put to the class.
Conductive loss in the right ear
Conductive loss on the right would give an ABNORMAL Rinne on the right — bone greater than air.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: Which headache patterns are EPISODIC, and which are UNILATERAL?
opts: All three are episodic and all three unilateral
Tension headache is not described as unilateral.
Only cluster is episodic and only tension unilateral
Cluster headache is not the only episodic one, and tension headache is not described as unilateral.
Migraine and tension are episodic; migraine and cluster are unilateral
Correct. Migraine appears in both lists, which is why the two features have to be taken together rather than either alone.
Migraine and cluster are episodic; migraine and tension are unilateral
The pairings are swapped.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: How does the nasal mucosa look in VIRAL rhinitis compared with ALLERGIC rhinitis?
opts: Viral is pale and bluish; allergic is red and swollen
Reversed. The pale bluish mucosa is the allergic picture; viral rhinitis makes it red and swollen.
Both are identical and cannot be distinguished
They are distinguishable, and mucosal colour is what separates them.
Viral is ulcerated; allergic is bleeding
Ulceration and bleeding are separate findings to look for, not the viral–allergic distinction.
Viral is red and swollen; allergic is pale, bluish or red
Correct. The pale bluish appearance is the one that points to allergy, and it is easy to miss if you are only looking for redness.

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set1.q: How long does benign positional vertigo last overall, as opposed to how long a single episode lasts?
opts: Episodes and the condition both last a few weeks
The defining feature of positional vertigo is precisely how BRIEF each episode is.
Each episode is under a minute, but the condition lasts a few weeks and may recur
Correct. The table separates the two timescales, and confusing them is the usual error.
Each episode is under a minute, and the condition resolves within 24 hours
Too short. The table gives a few weeks, with recurrence possible.
Episodes last hours, and the condition lasts a few weeks
Hours is the Ménière episode length.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Besides the whispered voice, which two bedside hearing screens are used?
opts: Weber and Rinne
These are the tuning fork tests, listed separately from the screens.
Finger rub and a watch
Correct — both are crude but immediately available, and both test whether any sound is heard at all.
Tuning fork and audiometry
The tuning fork tests distinguish the TYPE of loss; they are not screens for its presence, and audiometry is not a bedside screen.
Otoscopy and insufflation
Both examine the ear structurally rather than screening hearing.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What is tinnitus, by definition?
opts: Hearing loss confined to the high frequencies
That is the presbycusis pattern, not tinnitus.
A sensation of fullness or pressure in the ear
Aural fullness — a separate symptom, though it accompanies tinnitus in Ménière disease.
Sound perceived with no external source
Correct. The definition turns on the absence of an external stimulus, which is what separates it from any complaint about external sound.
A perception of rotation or spinning
That is vertigo.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Tinnitus WITH hearing loss and vertigo together points to which diagnosis?
opts: Benign positional vertigo
Positional vertigo has no tinnitus and does not affect hearing.
Acute labyrinthitis
Vestibular neuronitis leaves hearing unaffected and produces no tinnitus.
Otitis externa
A canal problem. It does not produce vertigo or tinnitus.
Ménière disease
Correct. Tinnitus with hearing loss AND vertigo together is Ménière; it is the combination that makes the diagnosis, not any one of the three.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which bacteria are named as the common causes of otitis media?
opts: Streptococcus pyogenes and Moraxella lacunata
Group A Streptococcus is given for pharyngitis, not otitis media.
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae
Correct — the two organisms named for this finding, and both are respiratory tract commensals that reach the middle ear through the Eustachian tube.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus
Those cause otitis EXTERNA, a canal infection.
Aspergillus niger and Candida albicans
The fungal causes of otitis externa.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A TENDER thyroid suggests what?
opts: Thyroiditis
Correct. Diffuse enlargement splits three ways on texture alone: soft is Graves, firm is Hashimoto, and tender is thyroiditis.
Graves disease
Graves is soft, not tender.
Endemic goitre
Endemic goitre is associated with iodine deficiency and is not described as tender.
A solitary cyst
A cyst presents as a single nodule.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which viral infections are listed as causes of SENSORINEURAL hearing loss?
opts: Rhinovirus and influenza
These cause upper respiratory infection, which contributes to serous effusion — a conductive problem.
Respiratory syncytial virus and adenovirus
Associated with otitis media, which is conductive.
Herpes simplex and varicella zoster
Herpes simplex and varicella zoster affect the ear in other ways; the two named congenital viral causes are rubella and cytomegalovirus.
Rubella and cytomegalovirus
Correct — both damage the inner ear, and both matter most when the exposure was congenital.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What kind of pressure is applied to the bulb during pneumatic otoscopy?
opts: A series of rapid repeated squeezes
One quick application is what the technique calls for.
Quick, firm but gentle
Correct. Only a small pressure change is needed; the membrane's movement is slight, and force adds nothing but discomfort.
Slow and sustained, held for several seconds
A sustained squeeze equalises rather than producing the brief deflection you are watching for.
As hard as the patient will tolerate
Force is not what makes the membrane move visibly, and it hurts.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which three findings together describe the tympanic membrane in acute otitis media?
opts: Red, retracted, and with the landmarks exaggerated
Retraction with exaggerated landmarks is the opposite picture — negative middle ear pressure pulling the membrane inward.
Pale, thickened and immobile
Thickening describes chronic change; the acute picture is redness and bulging.
Amber with visible bubbles
That is a serous effusion, without the redness of acute infection.
Red, bulging, and with the landmarks lost
Correct. The purulent effusion behind it pushes it outward and obscures the normal anatomy.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which cranial nerves carry referred pain to the ear?
opts: V, VII, IX and X
Correct. Four nerves supply sensation to the ear, which is exactly why disease well away from the ear can present as otalgia.
III, IV and VI
The ocular motor nerves. They have no sensory supply to the ear.
VIII alone
Cranial nerve VIII is vestibulocochlear — hearing and balance, not pain sensation.
XI and XII
Accessory and hypoglossal — motor nerves to the shoulder and tongue.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A tympanic membrane perforation that does NOT extend to the margin is called what?
opts: Traumatic
That describes the cause, not the position.
Central
Correct. The classification is simply by whether the margin is involved, and a marginal perforation is the one that does involve it.
Marginal
Marginal perforations are the ones that DO involve the margin.
Attic
Attic perforations are named in some classifications, but the split used here is simply central against marginal.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: How is the auricle positioned to straighten the ear canal for otoscopy in an adult?
opts: Press it forward against the cheek
This would close the canal rather than open it.
Leave it undisturbed and advance the speculum slowly
Without straightening the canal the speculum meets the canal wall, which is both painful and uninformative.
Pull it up, back, and away from the head
Correct — all three directions. The canal is not straight, and the view is only as good as the alignment.
Pull it down and back
That is the manoeuvre for an infant, whose canal runs differently.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Submandibular swelling and erythema with cellulitis of the floor of the mouth. What is it, and what is the danger?
opts: A peritonsillar abscess — the danger is rupture
A peritonsillar abscess deviates one tonsil; it is not a floor-of-mouth cellulitis.
A submandibular stone — the danger is infection
A stone causes obstruction and swelling at meals, not spreading cellulitis.
Ludwig's angina — it is life threatening because of the AIRWAY
Correct. The swelling pushes the tongue and floor of mouth upward and back, and the airway is the reason this cannot wait.
Ludwig's angina — the danger is spread to the mediastinum only
Mediastinal spread can occur, but the stated danger is the airway.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A MULTINODULAR enlarged thyroid carries a risk of malignancy under what circumstance?
opts: Always, regardless of history
A multinodular gland is usually a metabolic process; it is a family history that raises the concern about malignancy.
Only if the gland is tender
Tenderness points to thyroiditis.
Only in patients under thirty
Age is not the stated qualifier.
When there is a family history
Correct — the multinodular gland is usually a metabolic process, and family history is what raises the concern.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What frequency pattern does presbycusis take?
opts: Loss confined to the speech range, sparing higher and lower tones
The pattern is high-frequency loss, not a band-limited one.
Higher frequency loss
Correct, and it is why the complaint is about clarity rather than volume — the high registers carry the consonants.
Lower frequency loss
Low-tone loss belongs to Ménière disease.
All frequencies equally
The loss is not flat; it starts high.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which chain comes FIRST in the standard sequence for palpating the neck nodes?
opts: Submental
It comes after the submandibular nodes.
Deep cervical
Near the end of the sequence.
Preauricular

Correct. The sequence runs preauricular, postauricular, occipital, tonsillar, submandibular, submental, superficial cervical, posterior cervical, deep cervical, supraclavicular — following a route so none is missed.
Supraclavicular
That is last in the sequence.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A raised, shiny, slow-growing lesion on the auricle with visible telangiectasia. What should be suspected?
opts: A tophus
A hard crystalline nodule, not a shiny vascular lesion.
Basal cell carcinoma
Correct. Raised, shiny, telangiectatic and slow growing — and malignant, which is what separates it from the benign lumps in the same list.
A cutaneous cyst
Benign, and neither shiny nor telangiectatic.
A keloid
Scar tissue, typically at a site of previous injury or piercing.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Necrotising ulcerative gingivitis is known by which other names?
opts: Angular cheilitis, and perleche
Those are names for cracking at the corners of the mouth.
Aphthous stomatitis, and canker sores
Those name aphthous ulcers.
Vincent's angina, and trench mouth
Correct. The second name records where it was first described in numbers, in the trenches of the First World War.
Ludwig's angina, and quinsy
Ludwig's angina is a floor-of-mouth cellulitis; quinsy is a peritonsillar abscess.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: The tongue deviates to one side on protrusion. Which nerve is involved?
opts: Cranial nerve VII
The facial nerve supplies facial expression.
Cranial nerve XII
Correct. Asymmetric protrusion is the hypoglossal sign, and it is why the tongue is checked for midline position.
Cranial nerve X
Cranial nerve X gives uvular deviation and failure of the palate to rise.
Cranial nerve V
The trigeminal nerve supplies the muscles of mastication, not the tongue.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: What are the four Centor criteria?
opts: Fever, tonsillar exudates, swollen anterior cervical adenopathy, and PRESENCE of cough
Cough counts when it is ABSENT — a cough points away from streptococcal infection and toward a viral cause.
Fever, sore throat, headache and myalgia
A viral syndrome, not the Centor criteria.
Fever, trismus, uvular deviation and drooling
Those suggest a peritonsillar abscess rather than the scoring rule for pharyngitis.
Fever, tonsillar exudates, swollen anterior cervical adenopathy, and ABSENCE of cough
Correct. Three are things present and one is a thing absent, which is the part most often misremembered.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Why should dentures be removed during the oral examination?
opts: To allow the tongue blade to be inserted
The tongue blade is for seeing the posterior pharynx; the dentures come out so the mucosa beneath them can be inspected.
To let the patient speak more clearly during the history
The reason given is examination of the mucosa beneath.
To look underneath for ulcers and lesions
Correct. A denture hides exactly the mucosa most at risk from chronic irritation.
To assess the fit of the denture itself
Blood tracking into the orbit is not the reason given; the cartilage has no blood supply of its own and dies without its lining.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A DIFFUSELY enlarged, SOFT thyroid. Which condition does that suggest?
opts: Graves disease
Correct. Diffuse and soft is Graves; diffuse and firm is Hashimoto.
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Hashimoto gives a FIRM diffuse enlargement.
Thyroiditis
Thyroiditis is characterised by TENDERNESS.
A thyroid cyst
A cyst is a single nodule, not diffuse enlargement.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which epistaxis history suggests a SYSTEMIC problem rather than a local one?
opts: Recurrent bleeding, or bleeding and bruising elsewhere on the body
Correct. One nosebleed is local until proven otherwise; a pattern of bleeding at other sites changes the question entirely.
Bleeding from one nostril after digital trauma
That is the classic LOCAL cause.
Bleeding that follows a recent upper respiratory infection
Inflammation is listed among the local causes.
Bleeding in dry winter air
Dry mucosa is a local cause.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: How does the course of CENTRAL vertigo differ in duration from the peripheral causes?
opts: Always under one minute
That is benign positional vertigo.
Always several hours
That is the Ménière pattern.
Variable, but rarely continuous
Correct — the table's wording. It is a useful contrast because the peripheral causes each have a fairly characteristic duration.
Always continuous until treated
Central vertigo is described as variable but RARELY continuous, which is the contrast worth holding onto.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: A TENDER node and a HARD, FIXED node each suggest what?
opts: Tender suggests malignancy; hard and fixed suggests inflammation
Reversed. Sensorineural loss is the later-onset pattern, and conductive loss is the one that shows up from childhood to about forty.
Both suggest inflammation
Fixation is the malignant feature.
Both suggest malignancy
Tenderness points to an inflammatory cause.
Tender suggests inflammation; hard and fixed suggests malignancy
Correct. The two most informative qualities of a node are how it feels and whether it moves.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: At what age do conductive and sensorineural hearing loss typically begin?
opts: Conductive in childhood and young adulthood up to about forty; sensorineural in middle or later years
Correct, and the split is useful because it puts the prior probability in place before you touch a tuning fork.
Conductive in middle or later years; sensorineural in childhood
Reversed. Sensorineural loss is the later-onset pattern, and conductive loss is the one that shows up from childhood to about forty.
Both typically begin after sixty
Only the sensorineural pattern is described as a later-years onset.
Both typically begin in childhood
Only conductive loss is given the childhood-to-forty range.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: The soft palate fails to rise and the uvula deviates to the opposite side. Which nerve is affected?
opts: Cranial nerve XII — the uvula deviates toward the paralysed side
Cranial nerve XII moves the tongue, not the palate.
Cranial nerve IX, with the uvula deviating toward the lesion
Cranial nerve IX carries sensation from the pharynx; it is cranial nerve X that elevates the palate, and its paralysis gives this finding.
Cranial nerve VII, with asymmetric palatal elevation
The facial nerve does not elevate the palate.
Cranial nerve X — the uvula deviates AWAY from the paralysed side
Correct. The working side pulls unopposed, so the uvula points away from the lesion.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which three structures are inspected and palpated before the otoscope is picked up?
opts: The auricles, the mastoid and the tragus
Correct. Tenderness found here localises disease before anything is put into the canal, and tragal tenderness in particular points to the canal itself.
The tympanic membrane, the ossicles and the cochlea
None of these can be inspected or palpated from outside; the first is seen only through the otoscope.
The parotid gland, the temporomandibular joint and the zygomatic arch
Relevant to referred pain on history, but not the three structures named for inspection and palpation of the ear.
The preauricular, postauricular and occipital nodes
These are palpated in the neck examination.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Cracking and inflammation at the CORNERS of the mouth. What is this called?
opts: Angular cheilitis
Correct — one of three lip abnormalities to recognise, alongside angioedema and herpes simplex.
Angioedema
Angioedema is diffuse swelling, not cracking at the angles.
Herpes simplex
Herpes gives grouped vesicles, typically at the vermilion border rather than the angles.
Aphthous ulceration
Aphthous ulcers are on the mucosa inside the mouth.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Vertigo comes on when the patient rolls onto one side in bed, lasts under a minute, and hearing is unaffected. Which is it?
opts: Benign positional vertigo
Correct. Sudden onset on rolling onto the affected side or tilting the head up, a few seconds to under a minute, hearing not affected, tinnitus absent.
Ménière disease
Ménière runs several hours to a day or more, and hearing IS affected.
Vestibular neuronitis
Onset runs hours to as long as two weeks, not seconds.
Acoustic neuroma
Insidious, with impaired hearing on one side and tinnitus present.

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
set2.q: Which tuning fork is used for the hearing tests, and under what conditions?
opts: Any available fork, since only the comparison matters
The frequency is specified, and a low-frequency fork is felt as much as heard.
A 512 hertz fork — the smaller one — in a quiet room
Correct. The frequency matters because it sits in the speech range and rings long enough to compare two positions.
A 128 hertz fork — the larger one — in a quiet room
The larger low-frequency fork is used to test vibration sense, not hearing.
A 512 hertz fork, with background noise to mask the other ear
A quiet room is specified; masking with noise is not part of the technique.
